questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of buffer stock?
options: A minimum level of inventory held to guard against delays or unexpected demand
The stock level at which a new order is placed
The maximum stock a business will hold
The time between ordering and delivery
questions.why: Buffer stock is the safety net. The business intends never to go below it, and it exists to absorb a late delivery or a demand spike.
whyNot: That is the reorder level, which is higher.
That is the maximum stock level.
That is lead time.

questions.stem: Which term is defined as: the time between placing an order with a supplier and receiving the goods?
questions.why: Lead time determines how early you must reorder. The longer and less reliable it is, the more buffer stock you need.
whyNot: Buffer stock is the minimum level held.
The reorder level is the stock level that triggers an order.
JIT is an approach holding minimal stock.

questions.stem: Usage is 200 units a week, lead time is two weeks and buffer stock is 300 units. What is the reorder level?
questions.why: Reorder level = buffer + (lead time x usage) = 300 + (2 x 200) = 700 units, so the delivery arrives just as stock reaches the buffer.
whyNot: This appears to use one week of lead time rather than two.
This uses two weeks of usage without the buffer.
That is the buffer alone, with no allowance for lead time.

questions.stem: What is the main drawback of holding too much inventory?
options: Cash is tied up in goods sitting still, which worsens liquidity
Production stops because materials run out
questions.why: Stock is cash in another form. Excess stock worsens the acid test ratio, costs storage and insurance, and risks obsolescence.
whyNot: That is the consequence of too LITTLE stock.
Also a consequence of too little stock.
Bulk discounts are gained by buying more, not lost.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a benefit of just in time?
options: Minimal cash tied up in stock and no storage cost
A large safety net against supplier delay
questions.why: JIT frees the cash that would sit in inventory and removes storage and obsolescence costs. It also makes problems visible immediately rather than hiding them behind a stock pile.
whyNot: JIT removes the safety net, which is its main risk.
Smaller, more frequent orders usually lose bulk discounts.
JIT means more frequent, smaller deliveries.

questions.stem: Why is just in time close to unworkable for many Maldivian businesses?
options: Lead times are long and variable because goods arrive by sea and transfer between boats
questions.why: JIT depends on short, reliable lead times. Where weather can delay either leg of a two-stage sea journey, businesses deliberately hold large buffer stocks and accept the tied-up cash as the price of not running out.
whyNot: There is no such restriction.
They hold unusually large buffer stocks, for exactly this reason.
Both demand and supply are variable, which argues against JIT.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a category of waste that lean production aims to eliminate?
questions.why: Lean targets anything that adds cost without adding value: excess stock, defects, waiting time, unnecessary transport, over-production, over-processing and unused talent.
whyNot: Wages pay for value-adding work; lean reduces wasted effort, not employment as such.
Price is a revenue decision, not waste.
Demand is what the business exists to serve.

questions.stem: What decides whether a business should adopt JIT?
options: Supplier reliability and lead time, weighed against the cost of a stockout
The legal form of the business
questions.why: Close, reliable suppliers and predictable demand make JIT viable; distant or unreliable ones make it dangerous. The cost of a stockout is the other half: an inconvenience in one business, a closed operation in another.
whyNot: Legal form is irrelevant to stock policy.
Profitability does not determine whether supply is reliable.
Headcount is not the deciding factor.

questions.stem: On an inventory control diagram, what does a steeper downward slope indicate?
options: Stock is being used up more quickly
questions.why: The downward slope is the rate of usage. Steeper means faster consumption, which means reordering sooner or more often.
whyNot: Lead time is the horizontal gap before a delivery arrives.
Buffer stock is the flat minimum line.
A late delivery shows as the line dipping below the buffer.
